prompt: Quitanda's cache would run Valkey on ElastiCache. Why does this lesson practise on the Redis server Ubuntu packages?
hint: Think about what a client library sees.

choices.text: Valkey cannot be installed outside AWS
choices.why: Valkey is an open-source project anyone can run; the reason is that the two answer the same commands.

choices.text: Valkey speaks the Redis protocol and commands, so the same client and the same commands work on both
choices.why: Right. Valkey is a fork of Redis 7.2.4, and `SET`, `EXPIRE` and eviction behave the same way.

choices.text: moto contains a Redis server that the lesson reuses
choices.why: moto records a cache cluster and runs no cache at all.

choices.text: Redis is free, and Valkey is billed per node-hour
choices.why: The node-hour is ElastiCache's price for the machine, whichever engine runs on it; both engines are free software.

prompt: In the sheet, a `cache.r7g.large` costs 0.34880 USD an hour with Valkey and 0.43600 with Redis OSS. How many USD a month does Valkey save on one node, over 730 hours? Give two decimal places.
hint: Subtract the two prices, then multiply by the hours.

prompt: A cache holds 10 GB steadily all month and answers a modest number of small requests. Which is cheaper by the sheet, Serverless Valkey or two `cache.r7g.large` Valkey nodes?
hint: Serverless charges for what it holds, every hour.

choices.text: Serverless, which charges for requests rather than for machines
choices.why: It charges for requests and also for every GB-hour held: 10 × 0.133 × 730 is 970.90 USD for the data alone.

choices.text: The two nodes
choices.why: Right. Two nodes are 509.25 USD a month; Serverless holding 10 GB is 970.90 before a single request.

choices.text: Serverless, because a million ECPUs cost less than a cent
choices.why: The requests are the smallest line; the data held is the one that grows with this cache.

choices.text: They cost the same, since both are billed by the hour
choices.why: Nodes are billed per node-hour and Serverless per GB-hour; the units differ, and so do the totals.

prompt: Match each option to what sets it apart.
hint: Two of the engines are nearly the same program.

pairs.right: A fork of Redis 7.2.4, and the lowest node price
The same commands as Valkey, at 20% more per node
Billed by GB-hours held and by ECPUs

right_distractors: Billed by the terabyte its queries scan

prompt: In a replication group with cluster mode enabled, how does the client know which shard holds `product:p-101`?
hint: There are 16,384 of something.

choices.text: It sends every command to the primary endpoint, which passes it on to the right shard
choices.why: That is the picture of cluster mode disabled, where one primary holds everything.

choices.text: It hashes the key to a slot, and each slot belongs to one shard
choices.why: Right. The client computes the slot and sends the command straight to the shard that owns it.

choices.text: It tries the shards in turn until one has the key
choices.why: A miss would then cost a request per shard; the slot makes it one request.

choices.text: Shards are filled in turn, so it looks the key up in a directory
choices.why: There is no directory of keys; the slot is computed from the key itself.

prompt: A primary acknowledges a write and fails before sending it to its replica. Automatic failover promotes the replica. What became of the write?
hint: How does the copy reach the replica?

choices.text: The new primary replays it from the old primary's disk
choices.why: The replica has no access to the failed node; it has only what it had received.

choices.text: ElastiCache waits to promote until the write is copied
choices.why: The node that held the write has stopped answering; there is nothing to wait for.

choices.text: It is lost, because replication is asynchronous
choices.why: Right. For a cache that is acceptable, since the database still holds the truth.

choices.text: ElastiCache retries it against the new primary
choices.why: ElastiCache does not keep a client's writes; retrying is the client's job.

prompt: moto answers `create-replication-group` with `available` on the same line, an engine version of `None` and zones in `us-east-1`. What does that tell you about the group you designed?
hint: What did moto start behind the answer?

choices.text: That it would be ready within seconds on AWS
choices.why: moto waits for nothing; on AWS the status is `creating` for minutes first.

choices.text: That ElastiCache places São Paulo groups in Virginia's zones
choices.why: The zones are a detail of the imitation, not of AWS.

choices.text: That failover was tested as part of creating it
choices.why: Nothing was tested; `test-failover` itself fails inside moto with a 500.

choices.text: Only that the request was well formed
choices.why: Right. moto records the group and runs no cache, and the details it fills in are its own.

prompt: Which of these are true of a Memcached cluster on ElastiCache? Choose all that apply.
hint: Memcached has none of what a replication group adds.

choices.text: Each key lives on one node, chosen by the client's hash
choices.why: Yes. The nodes are independent and the client spreads the keys.

choices.text: A node that dies takes its keys with it
choices.why: Yes. Nothing is replicated, so nothing fails over.

choices.text: A replica in another zone is promoted when a node fails
choices.why: That is a Valkey or Redis OSS replication group with automatic failover.

choices.text: Its keys are split into 16,384 hash slots
choices.why: Hash slots are cluster mode, in Valkey and Redis OSS.

prompt: `redis-cli TTL product:p-101` answers `(integer) -2`. What does that mean?
hint: Compare it with the key `visits`, which answered `-1`.

choices.text: The key never expires
choices.why: That is `-1`, which the key `visits` answered.

choices.text: The key expires in two seconds
choices.why: A time left is a positive number; negative numbers are the two special answers.

choices.text: There is no such key, for example because it expired
choices.why: Right. After `sleep 6` the key had gone, `GET` answered `(nil)` and `TTL` answered `-2`.

choices.text: The key expired two seconds ago and is still readable
choices.why: An expired key is gone for every reader; `GET` answered `(nil)`.

prompt: `redis-cli SET product:p-101 '{...}' ___ 300` stores the value with a time to live of five minutes.
hint: The option is two letters, and `ex=` is its name in the Python client.

prompt: Why does the lesson run `sudo systemctl disable --now redis-server` straight after installing the package?
hint: What did the package start on its own?

choices.text: The package started a Redis service of its own, which would also start at every boot
choices.why: Right. Stopping it means nothing runs unless you start it, like moto.

choices.text: The packaged service writes to disk, and a cache must keep nothing
choices.why: Persistence is turned off by the flags you start Redis with; that is not why the service is stopped.

choices.text: Otherwise `redis-cli` would connect to ElastiCache
choices.why: `redis-cli` connects to `127.0.0.1:6379` unless told otherwise; it knows nothing of AWS.

choices.text: The packaged service refuses connections from Python
choices.why: Any client on the same machine can connect to it; the reason is that it runs when you did not start it.

prompt: Put the messages of a cache-aside read that misses in order.
hint: The cache never talks to the database.
items: The program sends `GET product:p-101` to the cache
The cache answers nil: the key is not there
The program runs the `SELECT` against the database
The program writes the answer with `SET ... EX 300`

prompt: The nightly import changed `p-101` to 1390 directly in the database, and the page still shows 1290. With no change to the import, what makes the page right?
hint: The cache did not hear about the change.

choices.text: Restarting `catalog.py`, which holds the price in a variable
choices.why: The program runs once per command and keeps nothing; the old price is in Redis.

choices.text: Reading the page again, since a hit refreshes the key from the database
choices.why: A hit returns what the cache holds and reads nothing from the database; that is what a hit is.

choices.text: Nothing until the key's time to live runs out
choices.why: Right. The TTL is the backstop: with 300 seconds, the page is wrong for at most five minutes.

choices.text: Redis notices the `UPDATE` and drops the key
choices.why: Redis and the database never talk to each other; nobody told the cache.

prompt: Why does `set_price` delete the cached key rather than write 1390 into it?
hint: Think of two writers changing the same price at almost the same moment.

choices.text: Writing the value would restart its time to live, so the copy would live too long
choices.why: A fresh copy with a fresh TTL is harmless; the danger is the older value winning.

choices.text: If two writers race to set it, the older value is left behind; a delete leaves nothing to be wrong
choices.why: Right. After a delete, the next reader fetches whatever the database holds.

choices.text: `DEL` is cheaper for Redis than `SET`
choices.why: Both are tiny; the choice is about correctness, not speed.

choices.text: Redis refuses `SET` on a key that already has a TTL
choices.why: `SET` replaces a key whatever it had, as `catalog.py` does on every miss.

prompt: The cache holds `p-101` at 1290. Which of these reads still goes to the database?
hint: Which one decides money?

choices.text: The photo and name on the product page
choices.why: Harmless a few minutes old, which is what a cache is for.

choices.text: The price charged at checkout
choices.why: Right. Charging a stale price is a bug with a refund attached.

choices.text: The price shown in a list of search results
choices.why: A page of results is a display, and the lesson caches exactly that; the charge is where the database decides.

choices.text: The list of categories in the menu
choices.why: Read all day and changed rarely: a good thing to cache.

prompt: Redis is at its `maxmemory` with the policy `noeviction`. What happens to a new `SET`?
hint: Read the name of the policy literally.

choices.text: It is accepted, and the least recently used key is evicted
choices.why: That is `allkeys-lru`.

choices.text: It is refused with an OOM error, and every existing key stays
choices.why: Right. `fill.py` counted 2,134 refusals, and `redis-cli` printed the error for a product's price.

choices.text: It is accepted, and the oldest keys are written to disk to make room
choices.why: Redis does not move keys to disk to make room; this server was even started with persistence off.

choices.text: It is accepted, and Redis grows past the limit
choices.why: The limit is enforced; that is what the 2 MB demonstration showed.

prompt: A program writes keys with no time to live into an ElastiCache cache on the default parameter group, until the cache is full. What happens next?
hint: The default policy is `volatile-lru`, and the lesson ran it on filler keys.

choices.text: The least recently used keys are evicted, whatever their expiry
choices.why: That is `allkeys-lru`; `volatile-lru` considers only keys that carry a TTL.

choices.text: ElastiCache adds a node to make room
choices.why: A node-based cache has the nodes you chose; adding one is your decision.

choices.text: Writes are refused, because no key is eligible for eviction
choices.why: Right. Locally, all 1,000 writes were refused under `volatile-lru`, exactly as under `noeviction`.

choices.text: ElastiCache gives each key a default TTL and expires the oldest
choices.why: No TTL is added for you; a key without one stays until it is deleted.

prompt: Why are login sessions a poor fit for a cache running `allkeys-lru`?
hint: What does the database have of a session?

choices.text: Session values are too large for Redis
choices.why: A session is a small value; size is not the problem.

choices.text: `allkeys-lru` refuses keys that carry a TTL
choices.why: It accepts any key and evicts any key; that is the trouble.

choices.text: Sessions change too often for a cache to keep up with
choices.why: Redis handles frequent writes well; what it does at its limit is the issue.

choices.text: A session is the original, and the cache is allowed to evict it, logging the user out
choices.why: Right. There is no copy to fall back on, unlike a product page.

prompt: In `herd.py`, why is the lock written with `ex=10` as well as `nx=True`?
hint: Imagine the request holding the lock crashes.

choices.text: So that the page itself expires after ten seconds
choices.why: The page is written with `ex=300`; `ex=10` belongs to the lock.

choices.text: So that a request that dies holding it cannot block the others for ever
choices.why: Right. After ten seconds the lock key is gone and another request can take it.

choices.text: Because `nx=True` is refused without an expiry
choices.why: `nx=True` works on its own; the expiry is a choice made for safety.

choices.text: So that ten requests at a time can hold it
choices.why: Exactly one request wins `nx=True`; the number is seconds.

prompt: Match each symptom to its cause.
hint: Each one was produced in this lesson or described by it.

pairs.right: A writer changed the database without deleting the key

pairs.left: Writes fail with an OOM error
pairs.right: The cache is full and its policy evicts nothing it holds

pairs.left: Users are logged out at random
pairs.right: Sessions live in a cache that evicts

pairs.left: The database spikes when one key expires
pairs.right: Every request that misses runs the same query

right_distractors: The replication group has cluster mode disabled

prompt: Which set of choices fits a cache of product pages that can always be rebuilt from the database?
hint: Everything in it is a copy.

choices.text: `noeviction`, no TTL, and writes going to the cache before the database
choices.why: That makes the cache the original and lets it fill until it refuses.

choices.text: `allkeys-lru`, a TTL on every key, and a delete on every write
choices.why: Right. Forgetting is harmless, the TTL bounds staleness, and the delete keeps writers honest.

choices.text: `volatile-lru`, no TTL, and the new value written into the cache on every change
choices.why: With no TTL, `volatile-lru` has nothing to evict and refuses writes when full.

choices.text: `allkeys-lru`, no TTL, and nothing done on writes
choices.why: A changed price would then stay wrong until the key happened to be evicted.

prompt: Which of these did this lesson actually run, rather than take from AWS's documentation? Choose all that apply.
hint: The real cache was the local Redis.

choices.text: Evictions under `allkeys-lru` at a 2 MB limit
choices.why: Yes, 3,039 of them, on the local Redis.

choices.text: Fifty simultaneous requests making one database read behind a lock
choices.why: Yes, with `herd.py lock`.

choices.text: A failover promoting a replica
choices.why: `test-failover` fails inside moto; failover was described from the documentation.

choices.text: ElastiCache's default `volatile-lru` parameter group
choices.why: The policy was run locally; that ElastiCache defaults to it comes from AWS's documentation.

choices.text: A Serverless cache growing on its own
choices.why: moto cannot create one at all; it answered with a 500.
